chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Two Ways Property Pays You

lessons.title: Income vs Growth: The Two Sources of Property Return

children.text: Two colleagues at an IT firm in Hinjewadi, Pune, invest in property in the same month. Priya buys a 2BHK flat in Wakad for ₹80 lakh and rents it out for ₹22,000 a month. Karan buys a residential plot in Talegaon for ₹40 lakh. It sits empty and pays nothing. Five years later, both say their investment worked. But they made money in completely different ways. Priya collected rent every month and watched the flat's price rise. Karan collected nothing, and the plot's entire gain exists only on paper until it is sold. By the end of this lesson you will be able to split any property's return into its two sources, calculate each one, and see why the split matters as much as the total.

body.text: Every rupee a property earns comes from one of two places: the rent it pays you while you own it, or the rise in its price when you sell it. Rent is a contract you can count on. Appreciation is a forecast you are hoping comes true.

children.text: Engine 1: Rental Yield

markDefs.definition: The rent a property earns in a year, expressed as a percentage of the property's price.

children.text: Rental yield

is the rent a property earns in a year, expressed as a percentage of what the property cost. It tells you how hard your money is working right now, the same way a dividend yield does for a stock like ITC or Coal India on NSE.

body.caption: Gross yield ignores costs. Net yield, which subtracts them, is covered in Chapter 2.

children.text: Priya's flat earns ₹22,000 × 12 = ₹2,64,000 a year. Divide by ₹80,00,000 and multiply by 100: a gross rental yield of 3.3%.
It arrives every month.
You do not need to sell anything to get paid.
It is written into a contract.
Residential rent agreements in India typically run for 11 months and often include a yearly increase of around 5%.
It needs a tenant.
An empty flat earns zero while EMIs, society maintenance and property tax keep running.
It is taxed every year.
Rent is taxed as income from house property in the year you receive it, after a 30% standard deduction.
Engine 2: Capital Appreciation

markDefs.definition: The increase in a property's market price over the time you own it.
A rise in value that exists only on paper because the asset has not been sold yet.

children.text: Capital appreciation
is the increase in the property's market price over time. Until you sell, it is only an
unrealised gain
: a number a broker quotes you, not money in your bank account.

body.caption: This is the total gain over your holding period, not a yearly figure.

children.text: Five years on, similar flats in Priya's society sell for ₹1.04 crore. The appreciation is (₹1,04,00,000 − ₹80,00,000) ÷ ₹80,00,000 × 100 = 30% over five years, which works out to about 5.4% a year compounded. Karan's plot is now worth about ₹60 lakh. That is 50% over five years, or about 8.4% a year, with no rent at all.
It arrives in one lump.
You get it only when you sell, and only if a buyer agrees to your price.
Nobody promises it.
It depends on jobs, infrastructure, interest rates and new supply in your micro-market, none of which you control.
It can be zero or negative.
Many buyers in parts of Noida and Gurugram who bought between 2012 and 2014 saw prices go nowhere for most of the following decade.
It is taxed only when you sell.
Hold for more than 24 months and the gain is long-term, taxed at 12.5% under current rules.

body.text: A broker telling you "your flat is now worth ₹1.1 crore" is not appreciation you have earned. Prices on 99acres or MagicBricks are asking prices, and deals often close below them. Your real appreciation is the price a buyer actually pays, minus what it costs you to sell.

columns.label: Rental yield
points: Paid monthly while you own the property
Needs a tenant; vacancy drops it to zero
Taxed every year as income from house property
Tells you what the property earns today

columns.label: Capital appreciation
points: Set by the market on the day you sell
Needs a buyer willing to pay your price
Taxed only on sale, as capital gains
Tells you what someone may pay tomorrow

children.text: Putting Both Engines Together

markDefs.definition: The combined gain from an investment: income received plus the change in its price.

children.text: Total return

is simply the two engines added together. Here is the five-year scorecard for Priya and Karan. To keep this first lesson clean, rent stays flat at ₹22,000 and we ignore stamp duty, maintenance, loans and tax. Every one of those gets added back later in the course.

body.caption: Five-year scorecard, before costs, loans and tax (illustrative)

cells: Total gain as % of purchase price

body.title: Where the Five-Year Gain Came From (₹ lakh)

children.text: Look at the shape of the return, not just the total. Karan's plot shows the higher percentage gain, but every rupee of it depends on selling at ₹60 lakh on the day Karan needs the money. More than a third of Priya's gain, ₹13.2 lakh, is already sitting in Priya's bank account. Now suppose Pune prices fall 10% in year five. Karan's gain shrinks from ₹20 lakh to ₹14 lakh. Priya's shrinks from ₹37.2 lakh to ₹26.8 lakh, but the rent already collected is untouched.

body.text: A property that relies on one engine carries all its risk in that engine. Rent cushions you against a bad year to sell. Appreciation rescues you from rent that barely beats inflation. The strongest property investments have a working version of both.

body.title: Calculate a gross yield
body.prompt: A 3BHK flat in Gachibowli, Hyderabad costs ₹1.2 crore and rents for ₹35,000 a month. What is its gross rental yield? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Annual rent = ₹35,000 × 12 = ₹4,20,000. Gross yield = ₹4,20,000 ÷ ₹1,20,00,000 × 100 = 3.5%. A ₹1.2 crore asset is earning ₹4.2 lakh a year, before a single rupee of cost.

children.text: The Two Engines Are Connected

markDefs.definition: A fall in rental yield that happens when property prices rise faster than rents.

children.text: Rent and price are not independent. Buyers pay more for a flat that can earn more rent, and rents rise when jobs arrive nearby. But the two rarely move at the same speed. When prices run ahead of rents, yield falls. This is called
yield compression
, and it is a big reason Indian residential yields are so low, which is exactly what the next lesson unpacks.

body.title: What happened to the yield?
body.question: Five years after purchase, Priya's flat has risen 30% in price to ₹1.04 crore, while rent has risen 15% to ₹25,300 a month. What has happened to the flat's gross rental yield at today's market price?
options: It cannot be calculated without the loan details
body.explanation: ₹25,300 × 12 = ₹3,03,600. Divided by ₹1,04,00,000, that is about 2.9%, down from 3.3%. Price grew faster than rent, so the yield compressed. Measured against Priya's original ₹80 lakh cost, the same rent is a 3.8% yield on cost. That is why long-time owners often feel their property pays well, even when a new buyer at today's price would earn much less.

children.text: Why the Split Matters for Your Cash Flow
Most Indians do not buy property with cash. Suppose Priya had funded the flat with a home loan of ₹64 lakh, 80% of the price, at 8.5% for 20 years. Here is what the monthly picture looks like.

body.title: Show me the math: Priya's EMI

content.caption: P = loan amount, r = monthly interest rate, n = number of monthly instalments

children.text: P = ₹64,00,000. r = 8.5% ÷ 12 = 0.7083% a month, or 0.007083. n = 20 × 12 = 240 months. (1 + r) raised to 240 is about 5.44. So EMI ≈ ₹64,00,000 × 0.007083 × 5.44 ÷ 4.44 ≈ ₹55,500. Rent of ₹22,000 leaves a gap of about ₹33,500 every month, and ₹22,000 ÷ ₹55,500 means rent covers roughly 40% of the EMI.

This is the everyday reality of growth-first property investing in India. The owner funds the gap from salary for years, betting that appreciation will more than repay it. That bet can work. But it is a bet on the second engine, and you should make it knowingly, not because a sample flat looked nice. Try your own numbers below.
Which Engine Do You Need?

The right mix depends on who you are, not on which number looks bigger in a brochure. A 30-year-old with a rising salary can absorb a monthly shortfall and wait for growth. A retiree who needs cash to live on cannot spend appreciation. This is also why REITs listed on NSE and BSE appeal to income seekers: SEBI requires them to distribute at least 90% of their net distributable cash flows. We cover REITs in Chapter 5.

body.title: Income or growth for a retiree?
body.scenario: Mrs. Lakshmi, a 62-year-old retired school teacher in Chennai, has ₹90 lakh from selling an ancestral house. The goal is steady monthly income to add to a pension. Option A: a 2BHK flat on OMR for ₹90 lakh, expected to rent at ₹21,000 a month, in an area where prices have been rising with the IT corridor. Option B: a small shop in T. Nagar for ₹90 lakh, already leased to a mobile phone retailer at ₹45,000 a month.
body.prompt: Which engine matters more for Mrs. Lakshmi? Calculate the gross yield on each option and list what should be checked before deciding.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The first engine, rental yield, matters more. Mrs. Lakshmi needs monthly cash, not a gain that arrives only on sale.
2. Option A: ₹21,000 × 12 = ₹2,52,000, a gross yield of 2.8%. Option B: ₹45,000 × 12 = ₹5,40,000, a gross yield of 6%. The shop pays more than twice as much every month.
3. The OMR flat may appreciate faster, but Mrs. Lakshmi would benefit only by selling, which defeats the purpose of buying for income.
4. Before choosing the shop, check the tenant's track record, the lease lock-in period, the annual escalation, the security deposit, how long a vacancy might last, and the shop's maintenance and property tax. A 6% yield from an unreliable tenant can be worse than 2.8% from a steady one.
5. Compare both with lower-risk income options such as the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme and bank FDs, which currently pay well above 2.8% with no tenant risk.

body.title: Paper or cash?
body.textWithBlank: Until you sell, capital appreciation is only an ___ gain.
body.explanation: Appreciation becomes real money only when a buyer pays your price. Until then it is an unrealised gain, and it can shrink or disappear.

cards.definition: A year's rent as a percentage of the property's price.
Annual rent ÷ property price × 100, before deducting any costs.
The rise in a property's market price over the time you own it.
A rise in value that exists only on paper until the asset is sold.
Income received plus the change in price over the holding period.
A fall in rental yield caused by prices rising faster than rents.
Current annual rent divided by what you originally paid, rather than today's market price.

points: Every property return comes from two engines: rent while you own it, and price appreciation when you sell.
Gross rental yield = annual rent ÷ property price × 100. An ₹80 lakh Wakad flat renting at ₹22,000 a month yields 3.3%.
Appreciation stays unrealised until a buyer pays your price, and it can be zero or negative.
Two properties with similar total gains can carry very different risks depending on which engine does the work.
When prices rise faster than rents, yield falls. This yield compression is a big reason Indian residential yields are low.
A low yield funded by a home loan means covering a monthly gap from salary, which is a deliberate bet on appreciation.
Match the engine to your need: income seekers should weight yield, while long-horizon earners can lean on growth, knowingly.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The people, properties, prices and rents are illustrative. Property values, loan rates and tax rules change, so verify current figures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser or a chartered accountant before making any decision.
